claims.text: Combining mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering can reduce the required sintering temperature for powder-based metallic alloys.
The MA+SPS process can retain mechanical properties comparable to those obtained by conventional sintering.
Machine-learning-guided optimization of SPS parameters contributes to lowering the sintering temperature while retaining mechanical properties.
The initially standard-processed powder has relatively coarse grains and fewer defects than mechanically alloyed powder.
Mechanical alloying introduces a high density of defects into the powder.
Mechanical alloying produces refined nanoscale powder.
A machine-learning workflow can identify optimized SPS temperature, pressure, and hold time.
Conventional sintering or hot pressing of similar powder-based alloys typically requires temperatures around or above 1400 °C and long dwell times.
Mechanical alloying produces a nanocrystalline microstructure.
Mechanical alloying increases defect density and grain-boundary area.
The nanocrystalline, defect-rich structure facilitates rapid densification during SPS.
Defects introduced by mechanical alloying increase atomic-diffusion pathways.
SPS rapidly heats and presses the powder.
Powder refinement by MA and rapid heating and pressure during SPS jointly enhance densification at lower temperatures.
Machine-learning parameter selection can balance phase stability and mechanical integrity.
The proposed process could reduce the required sintering temperature by about 200 °C or more.
The proposed lower-temperature process can achieve near-full densification.
The proposed process can retain mechanical performance comparable to conventionally sintered material.
The approach is expected to be effective across powder-based systems to which mechanical alloying can be applied.
The magnitude of temperature reduction and property retention may depend on alloy composition, processing equipment, and the accuracy of SPS parameter optimization.
